title: SYNDACTYLY, TYPE III
alt_titles: SYNDACTYLY OF FINGERS IV AND V

intro.text: This entry describes type III syndactyly (SDTY3), an autosomal dominant malformation in which the ring and little fingers are joined. Type III syndactyly can occur on its own or as part of oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODDD). A family with type III syndactyly was linked to the ODDD region on chromosome 6q22-q24, which contains the GJA1 gene.

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly (SDTY3) is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
checks.evidence_quote: The present family provides evidence of the variable expression in oculodentodigital dysplasia. Inheritance is autosomal dominant.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives autosomal dominant inheritance for this single family, which it treats as showing ODDD's variable expression. It does not make a general statement about type III syndactyly.

checks.claim: In type III syndactyly (SDTY3), the ring and little fingers are joined.
checks.evidence_quote: all three patients exhibit characteristic facies that includes thin and narrow noses, underdeveloped/thin nostrils, and/or prominent bridges in addition to syndactyly of the fourth and fifth digits of the hands

(2016) (PMID 27226478) describing PMID 2157843, not the paper's own text; the claim was not checked against PMID 2157843 itself. Verdict on the later paper's description: partially_supported. The abstract does not define type III syndactyly. Only a later citing paper (Kelly et al.) mentions fourth and fifth finger syndactyly, and it describes the patients rather than defining the condition.

checks.explanation: The paper places GJA1 at 6q22-q23 within the ODDD candidate region, but it does not define that region as 6q22-q24.

paragraphs.text: Type III syndactyly is a malformation of the hands in which the ring (fourth) and little (fifth) fingers are joined. It is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait and its expression varies (Johnston and Kirby, 1955; McKiernan and McCann, 1993; De Smet et al., 1994). The fifth finger often has a short middle phalanx (brachymesophalangia) (De Smet et al., 1994). Type III syndactyly can occur on its own or as part of oculodentodigital dysplasia (Gladwin et al., 1997; Paznekas et al., 2003).

checks.evidence_quote: Syndactyly of the ring and little finger.
checks.explanation: The title describes syndactyly of the ring and little fingers. Jordan et al. also describe type III as syndactyly between the fourth and fifth fingers.

checks.claim: Type III syndactyly is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.
checks.evidence_quote: involving 7 affected males and 7 affected females over 5 generations in a pattern compatible with an autosomal dominant inheritance
checks.explanation: Second-hand: the evidence is a paragraph of Jordan et al. (2012) (PMID 22448207) describing PMID 14361398, not the paper's own text; the claim was not checked against PMID 14361398 itself. Verdict on the later paper's description: supported. Jordan et al. (a second-hand description) report that this family's pattern fits autosomal dominant inheritance. Cassim et al. also list it as AD.

checks.explanation: The abstract reports variable expression.

checks.evidence_quote: Brachymesophalangia of the fifth finger is a frequent association.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

paragraphs.text: Type III syndactyly is also called the Johnston-Kirby type, after the family reported by Johnston and Kirby (1955).

Cassim et al. call type III the Johnston-Kirby type and cite this paper for it.

paragraphs.text: Opjordsmoen and Nyberg-Hansen (1980) reported a family from northern Norway with a hereditary neurologic disorder made up of spastic paraplegia, neurogenic bladder disturbance and syndactyly. Nine of 22 family members across 3 generations had these features. The bladder disturbance was an incomplete supranuclear bladder paresis (uninhibited neurogenic bladder). It was the main complaint and appeared early in the disease. The authors thought the family probably had an unusual form of hereditary spastic paraplegia.

checks.explanation: Stated directly in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Brueton et al. (1990) described a family with type III syndactyly whose facial appearance resembled that of oculodentodigital dysplasia. None of the other characteristic findings of oculodentodigital dysplasia were present. The authors discussed whether type III syndactyly and oculodentodigital dysplasia are separate genetic entities or part of one disease spectrum.

paragraphs.text: Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) reported a newborn boy with complete cutaneous syndactyly of fingers 3 to 5 on the left hand and fingers 4 and 5 on the right hand. His mother and maternal grandmother had been born with the same hand malformation. The mother had a thin nose and small teeth, and her eyes were normal. The grandmother's teeth had been very small, with enamel hypoplasia, and her eyes were normal. The authors considered that the family showed the variable expression of oculodentodigital dysplasia.

paragraphs.text: McKiernan and McCann (1993) reported a pedigree with 14 cases of familial syndactyly of the ring and little fingers. Three of the patients were treated surgically in the authors' unit. A fourth had been treated elsewhere earlier by the senior author. Clinical study showed that expression varied.

paragraphs.text: De Smet et al. (1994) described 5 new cases of isolated syndactyly of the ring and little fingers. A short middle phalanx of the fifth finger (brachymesophalangia) was a frequent associated finding. The authors stated that surgery is needed at a young age.

paragraphs.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance of type III syndactyly was shown by the 5-generation family of Johnston and Kirby (1955). It was also supported by the families reported by Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993), McKiernan and McCann (1993) and De Smet et al. (1994). Opjordsmoen and Nyberg-Hansen (1980) considered the inheritance autosomal dominant in their family with spastic paraplegia, neurogenic bladder disturbance and syndactyly.

checks.claim: Autosomal dominant inheritance of type III syndactyly was shown by the 5-generation family of Johnston and Kirby (1955).
checks.evidence_quote: involving 7 affected males and 7 affected females over 5 generations in a pattern compatible with an autosomal dominant inheritance
checks.explanation: Second-hand: the evidence is a paragraph of Jordan et al. (2012) (PMID 22448207) describing PMID 14361398, not the paper's own text; the claim was not checked against PMID 14361398 itself. Verdict on the later paper's description: partially_supported. The family spans 5 generations, but Jordan et al. say only that the pattern is 'compatible with' autosomal dominant inheritance. The draft's 'shown' is stronger than that.

checks.claim: Autosomal dominant inheritance of type III syndactyly was supported by the family reported by Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993).
checks.evidence_quote: The mother and maternal grandmother were born with the same hand malformation. Facial features in the mother showed a thin nose and small teeth; eyes were normal.
checks.explanation: The family shows three affected generations, and the paper says 'Inheritance is autosomal dominant.' That sentence is not tied explicitly to type III syndactyly as opposed to ODDD; the link comes only from the title.

checks.evidence_quote: The mode of inheritance is considered to be autosomal dominant.
checks.explanation: Stated directly in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Gladwin et al. (1997) ran a genome-wide search in families with oculodentodigital syndrome and found linkage to polymorphic markers on chromosome 6q (pairwise Zmax = 9.37; theta = 0.001). They also analyzed a large family with type III syndactyly and atypical facial features. This analysis suggested that the locus for isolated type III syndactyly lies in the same region, 6q22-q24.

checks.claim: Gladwin et al. (1997) ran a genome-wide search in families with oculodentodigital syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: In the current investigation, a total genome search for the location of the ODD locus was instigated
checks.explanation: A total genome search for the ODD locus matches the claim. That it was done in families follows from the linkage analysis.

checks.claim: Gladwin et al. (1997) found linkage of oculodentodigital syndrome to polymorphic markers on chromosome 6q (pairwise Zmax = 9.37; theta = 0.001).
checks.evidence_quote: linkage to polymorphic markers located on chromosome 6q established (pairwise Zmax = 9.37; theta = 0.001)
checks.explanation: The markers, chromosome and statistics all match.

checks.claim: Gladwin et al. (1997) analyzed a large family with type III syndactyly and atypical facial features.
checks.evidence_quote: Analysis of a large family with type III syndactyly, but atypical facial features
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Analysis by Gladwin et al. (1997) of a large family with type III syndactyly suggested that the locus for isolated type III syndactyly lies in the same region as oculodentodigital syndrome, 6q22-q24.
checks.evidence_quote: further suggested that isolated type III syndactyly is also located in this same region of the genome.
checks.explanation: The title gives the region as 6q22-q24, and the abstract says isolated type III syndactyly lies in the same region.

paragraphs.text: Whether isolated type III syndactyly is a separate entity from oculodentodigital dysplasia has been discussed. Brueton et al. (1990) raised the question of whether the two are separate genetic entities or a single disease spectrum. Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) took their family with type III syndactyly and mild dental and nasal features as evidence that oculodentodigital dysplasia varies in expression. In contrast, De Smet et al. (1994) described type III syndactyly as an isolated malformation. Gladwin et al. (1997) noted that type III syndactyly occurs as part of oculodentodigital syndrome but has also been reported on its own. Their linkage data suggested that the two map to the same region of chromosome 6q.

checks.claim: Whether isolated type III syndactyly is a separate entity from oculodentodigital dysplasia has been discussed.
checks.evidence_quote: The relationship between type III syndactyly and oculodentodigital dysplasia is discussed.
checks.explanation: The paper discusses whether the two are separate entities.

checks.claim: Brueton et al. (1990) raised the question of whether type III syndactyly and oculodentodigital dysplasia are separate genetic entities or a single disease spectrum.
checks.evidence_quote: Oculodentodigital dysplasia and type III syndactyly: separate genetic entities or disease spectrum?
checks.explanation: The title raises exactly this question.

checks.claim: Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) took their family with type III syndactyly and mild dental and nasal features as evidence that oculodentodigital dysplasia varies in expression.
checks.evidence_quote: Facial features in the mother showed a thin nose and small teeth; eyes were normal. In the grandmother, teeth had been very small with enamel hypoplasia; eyes were normal. The present family provides evidence of the variable expression in oculodentodigital dysplasia.
checks.explanation: The mild dental and nasal features and the authors' conclusion about variable expression are both stated in the abstract.

checks.evidence_quote: Type III syndactyly, which occurs as part of ODD, has also been reported to occur as an isolated entity.

checks.claim: Linkage data of Gladwin et al. (1997) suggested that type III syndactyly and oculodentodigital syndrome map to the same region of chromosome 6q.
checks.evidence_quote: further suggested that isolated type III syndactyly is also located in this same region of the genome.
checks.explanation: The abstract places ODD on 6q and suggests isolated type III syndactyly maps to the same region.

paragraphs.text: Paznekas et al. (2003) noted that the connexin-43 gene, GJA1, lies on chromosome 6q22-q23 within the candidate region for oculodentodigital dysplasia. They found GJA1 mutations in all 17 families with oculodentodigital dysplasia that they screened: 16 different missense mutations and 1 codon duplication. They stated that type III syndactyly can occur in some cases of oculodentodigital dysplasia.

checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.evidence_quote: Sixteen different missense mutations and one codon duplication were detected.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.evidence_quote: Syndactyly type III and conductive deafness can occur in some cases, and cardiac abnormalities are observed in rare instances.
